indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B2.1.1.2: Understand the differences between living, non-living things and things which have never been alive
indicator.objective: Group things collected from the environment into living and non-living things

skills.description: Sort collected items into living and non-living things
Give a simple reason for grouping an item as living or non-living
Give examples of living and non-living things from the environment
Draw and colour some of the things collected

misconceptions: Non-living things are the same as dead things.
Things made from plants (e.g., a wooden table) are living because they come from trees.
Things that do not move (e.g., a tree) are non-living.

questions.stem: Is a dog living or non-living?
questions.explanation: A dog is a living thing because it eats, breathes, grows, and reproduces.
questions.misconception: Pupils may classify animals as non-living if they are thinking of a toy dog.

questions.stem: Is a stone living or non-living?
questions.explanation: A stone is a non-living thing.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think stones are living because they are part of the environment.

questions.stem: Which of these is a living thing?
questions.explanation: A tree is a living thing.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cars are living because they move.

questions.stem: Which of these is a non-living thing?
questions.explanation: A cup is a non-living thing.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think everything in the house is living.

questions.stem: Kwame collected a leaf, a stone, and a worm. Which one is living?
hints: Which one moves on its own?
questions.explanation: A worm is a living thing. A leaf from a tree is no longer living once it falls, and a stone is non-living.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a leaf is living because it came from a tree.

questions.stem: Why is a tree classified as a living thing?
hints: What does it do over time?
What does it need to survive?
questions.explanation: A tree is living because it grows, needs water and air, and reproduces.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think trees are non-living because they do not move.

questions.stem: Ama collected a stone, a leaf, a bottle, and a snail. Which group has only non-living things?
hints: Which two have never been alive?
One is from the ground, one is man-made.
questions.explanation: A stone and a bottle are non-living things.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a leaf is non-living because it is no longer on the tree, but a fallen leaf is still considered living or once-living. A bottle is clearly non-living.

questions.stem: Why is a chair non-living?
options: It does not grow or eat
questions.explanation: A chair is non-living because it cannot grow, eat, breathe, or reproduce.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a wooden chair is living because it comes from a tree.

questions.stem: Is a wooden table living or non-living?
options: Living, because it comes from a tree
hints: Can a table grow new branches?
It is no longer a tree.
questions.explanation: A wooden table is non-living. Even though the wood came from a tree, the table itself cannot grow, eat, or breathe.
questions.misconception: Pupils often think wooden objects are living because they were once part of a tree.

questions.stem: Ama says 'A car is living because it moves.' Why is she wrong?
options: A car does not grow or reproduce
hints: Can a car have baby cars?
questions.explanation: A car is non-living because, although it moves, it cannot grow, eat, breathe, or reproduce.
questions.misconception: Pupils often think movement is the only sign of life.

questions.stem: Sort these items into living and non-living: dog, stone, tree, cup.
answer: living: dog, tree; non-living: stone, cup
living: dog tree, non-living: stone cup
questions.explanation: A dog and a tree are living. A stone and a cup are non-living.
questions.misconception: Pupils may group items by size or location instead of living vs non-living.

questions.stem: Name one living thing and one non-living thing you can see in your school.
answer: living: tree, grass, bird, pupil, teacher, dog; non-living: stone, desk, chair, building, car
questions.explanation: A tree is a living thing, and a desk is a non-living thing.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name only animals for living things.

questions.stem: Kofi picked up a dead branch from the ground. Is it living or non-living?
options: Living, because it was once on a tree
hints: It is no longer part of a living tree.
questions.explanation: A dead branch is non-living. It was once part of a living tree, but now it is dead.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think wood is always living.

questions.stem: Explain why a stone is non-living but a dog is living.

criteria.description: States a dog grows, eats, or breathes
States a stone does not grow, eat, or breathe

hints: What does the dog do that the stone cannot?
questions.explanation: A dog is living because it grows, eats, and breathes. A stone is non-living because it does none of these things.

questions.stem: Ama collected a flowing river, a bird, a stone, and grass. Which is living?
hints: A river moves but does it grow?
questions.explanation: A bird and grass are living things. A river flows but is non-living, and a stone is non-living.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a flowing river is living because it moves.

questions.stem: Why do we group things into living and non-living things?
options: To make them easier to carry
To understand the world around us
hints: Think about how scientists organise things.
It helps us learn about nature.
questions.explanation: We group things into living and non-living to help us understand and study the world around us.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think grouping is just for sorting objects physically.

questions.stem: Draw one living thing and one non-living thing you collected from outside.
hints: A leaf or a bug could be living.
A stone or a piece of plastic is non-living.
questions.explanation: This tests observation and classification through drawing.

questions.stem: Write two differences between a living thing and a non-living thing.

criteria.description: States living things grow, non-living do not
States living things need food/water/air, non-living do not

hints: Think about how you change as you grow.
questions.explanation: Living things grow and need food/water/air. Non-living things do not.

questions.stem: A candle flame moves and uses up fuel. Why is it NOT a living thing?
options: It does not grow or have cells
hints: Can a flame grow into a bigger flame and have baby flames?
It does not have a body like a plant or animal.
questions.explanation: A candle flame is not living because it does not grow, reproduce, or consist of cells, even though it moves and uses fuel.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think anything that moves or 'uses' something is alive.

questions.stem: Go outside and collect three things. Show them to your teacher and say whether each is living or non-living.

criteria.description: Correctly classifies at least two items as living or non-living

hints: Pick up a stone, a leaf, or a seed.
questions.explanation: This tests real-world observation and classification.
